newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs pull out of strategic town arbitration.
newsitem.headline: Serbs pull out of strategic town arbitration.

text.p: Bosnian Serbs announced on Sunday they were pulling out of arbitration designed to determine control over the strategically important town of Brcko.
They said they had withdrawn their representative from a sensitive arbitration panel and "Republika Srpska does not intend to participate any longer in such an arbitration proceeding".
The decision caught diplomats in Sarajevo by surprise and one termed it "a very worrying development".
Brcko sits astride the Posavina Corridor in northern Bosnia, a narrow strip of land which links the eastern and western halves of the Serbs' Republika Srbska.

Bosnian government forces failed to cut the corridor during the war and Serbs are determined to prevent the Moslem-Croat Federation from gaining control of even a substantial part of Brcko through arbitration.
The Dayton peace accord ended 43 months of war in Bosnia a year ago but left the status of Brcko unresolved. The agreement called for a three-member panel to arbitrate the issue.
One member was appointed by the Federation, which controls 51 percent of Bosnia, and a second by Republika Srpska, which administers the other 49 percent.
The third arbitrator, agreed by the other two, is American attorney Roberts Owen, who serves as the panel's presiding officer.

"We wish to inform you that the Republika Srpska wishes to revoke its decision to appoint Dr. Vitomir Popovic as its chosen member of the arbitral panel..,," said a letter from Republika Srpska Prime Minister Gojko Klickovic to Owen.
A copy of the letter, dated December 1, was made available to Reuters.

It accused Owen of siding with the Federation, saying: "Through your actions you clearly showed that ... you intend to use the tribunal and the arbitration process as a smokescreen for the imposition of a pre-ordained, unjust decision ...."
Informed of the letter, the office of the international community's top civilian in Bosnia, Carl Bildt, reacted with concern.
"If this is true it is not helpful to the process," said Colum Murphy, Bildt's spokesman in Sarajevo.
"Brcko is such a serious issue and a casus belli that we will be looking at this matter closely in coming days."
Although the arbitration has been conducted behind closed doors, diplomatic sources say there has been little progress.
"Popovic generally avoided meetings. There may have been one meeting in August in Vienna where all three parties were present, but even that's in doubt," said a Western diplomat.
Rumours of secret meetings among Moslem, Serb and Croat leaders to try to sort out the Brcko problem have been impossible to confirm.
Dayton called for a final decision on Brcko not later than December 13, but sources close to the arbitration say an extension of 60 days is likely to be announced soon.
